text:
Interviewee: Three and a half years.
Interviewer: What happened then to interrupt it?
Interviewee: What do you mean? We didn’t have to.. Well, the war — we didn’t have the right to... it was the war.
Interviewee: You have no Jewish people...Even they had the star, the yellow star, the right to go, like people are going all around.. in the middle.. but to go to school — to attend te school — there was no question about it...
Interviewer: By this time it was 1938.
Interviewee: I don’t know.
Interviewer: And the Germans had invaded Poland.
Interviewee: Of course.
Interviewer: How quickly did your life change after the Germans invaded Poland?
Interviewee: We were in the ghetto.
Interviewer: When did they really start...?
Interviewee: Right away. We.. my parents had a beautiful apartment and everything was comfortable. You know...And, uh.. they came.. we had a chandelier.. they took the chandelier.. we had a velvet drapes.. they didn’t ask you.
Interviewer: They just took...
Interviewee: Yah. And, I was sitting and reading a scene all my life. And he said, “Du seine ein schawshpeiler?” are you an actree?
Interviewer: Younger than you? You are the oldest?
Interviewee: Yah, the oldest.
Interviewer: How much older are you than your sister and your brothers?
Interviewee: No, one after another, you know.
Interviewer: Close together in age?
Interviewee: Yah, close. Very close. My sister is a year and a half younger. I’ll show you my pictures. Terrible, terrible.
Interviewer: There was not enough food? Was there enough water? Were people moved into your home?
Interviewee: No, no, no. This anti-Semitism was in the Polish government. What I told you.. And, after, when the Germans came, it was much worse. Much worse.
Interviewer: But after the Germans came, it was much worse.
Interviewee: It was much worse. We have been separated from people, anyway. Maybe I didn’t make clear.
Interviewer: Can you describe the ghetto — was there really an actual wall?
Interviewee: There was ein bridge. Yes, it was a wall, and there were soldiers staying on.. in front of the door — called traver hoffen, and when you used to come fro work.. they used to.. when we used to.. in the morning — 5 o’clock in the morning they used to serve us.. let me tell it from the beginning...
Interviewer: Go ahead.
Interviewee: They used to serve us coffee from the previous kettle. The kettle was for soup. The soup was from stained bread. And, in the coffee was still alive worms. And that is what we went.. we went through this, and I was...when we have to come to work, then we have to stay by the soldiers in a row.
Interviewer: What kind of work did you have to do?
Interviewee: Whatever they give us.
Interviewer: Well, for instance.
Interviewee: I was carrying heavy canisters. Is it canisters in English? Canisters.
Interviewer: Canisters.
Interviewee: Canisters. Very heavy canisters. They were like that. We Carried this to put in the train. This what I do. And
Interviewer: How did you have the strength to do this with so little food?
Interviewee: You know...then there was a head from a horse, with the teeth together. Did you hear of this?
Interviewer: I heard of similar things.. but it is still unpleasant.
Interviewee: And, in the morning, how you call this.. the coffee.. or the coup.. no, what was coffee.. because the kettle wasn’t clean.. contained stained bread, which was the soup at 12 o’clock and she used to pour, she used to pour like this. Everything here, and nothing was left.
Interviewer: You mean the person who was dishing it out? And they would pour it out so it would spill?
Interviewee: Anyway, this was.. and in the evening there was this head. Piece of head with the teeth.
Interviewer: You must have become very thin with such a diet?
Interviewee: Some diet. Didn’t you hear about that?
Interviewer: Yes, but I still want to hear..
Interviewee: No, no, no. But.. do you want to talk about it?
Interviewer: Certainly, we’ll talk about it.
Interviewee: Yah. I was in Kaiservald. Kaiserland is Riga, Latvia. You want to know that?
Interviewer: Yes, I do want to know that. When did you go there? Do you remember?
Interviewee: I don’t remember the year. 1942.
Interviewer: 1942. How did you go there? How did they get you from Vilna?
Interviewee: By transportation — not cars, of course. Cattle.. cattle trains.
Interviewer: Can you describe it?
Interviewee: Yes, I can describe it. One on top another and all the physiological needs was done right there. You understand what I mean?
Interviewer: Yes I understand. There was no toilet facility.
Interviewee: Water, also.
Interviewer: How many days did that trip take?
Interviewee: Who knows... it was about nine days, and, let me tell you, some people couldn’t stand it. they broke the window ad fell out and break their arms and their legs.
Interviewer: And some of the people died while they were on the train?
Interviewee: No, they don’t die. They didn’t want to go. They didn’t want to leave, and they broke the windows. It was in the train a window, a cattle train. Even the boards, they used to..
Interviewer: Didn’t they give you any food during this time, or did you have food..?
Interviewee: We didn’t have even water.
Interviewer: For nine days. You must have been frantic by the time you got to the camp.
Interviewee: The worst thing is the odor. Ach!
Interviewer: What did they tell you about.. what did they say about where you were going to?
Interviewee: They didn’t talk with us. When we came already to the destination place, it was the whole room.. full of little mattresses full of straw.. one on top of the other. An then they brought something, I don’t know, what kind of straw. I am not a good.. I am a very big picker, since I was young, very young at home, I couldn’t tough this.. I couldn’t tough this.. this kind of food.
Interviewer: And, what kind of tasks did they have you doing at Kaiservald?
Interviewee: In Kaiservald? I told you, I was on the rampus. How is rampus in English?
Interviewer: You had your own child then?
Interviewee: No, she wasn’t born yet. What I want to say? And, then it was terrible because we heard that in the ghetto, people hanged themselves.. full of them.. I came to this main man.. Do you remember the name of this main man...I forgot.. Katle.. Katle. I said, “Listen, I know how, and I said that we know how to sew for the invalids and everything.” And he said we should stay in toor vacher — that’s a place there what he showed to me, “and then I’ll talk to you” But, he never came. We never talked. And then we took...Then we had on the field...
Interviewer: Then, what did you do? He told you to wait?
Interviewee: Yah, they come.. they took us.
Interviewer: So then you went down to the train?
Interviewee: No, not right away to the train. It was night already. It was Pilsudski very big.. a big, big space.. it doesn’t make sense, I don’t know... I jump form one to another. How could you do something with that?
Interviewer: That’s all right. Just keep talking. So let’s go.
Interviewee: They brought us back..
Interviewer: To Kaiservald?
Interviewee: No, they brought us back.. first of all, over night, and then they put us again in the cattle train. From the ghetto to sleep over somewhere in the field and then from the.. in the morning.. everybody.. they took us to the cattle train, and from the cattle train to the Kaiservald.
Interviewer: When you got to Kaiserlaut there were mattresses with straw?
Interviewee: They gave us.. what did they give us? Soup. Soup.
Interviewer: Did people who worked in the kitchens, for instance, have a little more to eat because they could take food for themselves?
Interviewee: The people worked in the kitchens very seldom. Only to wash sometimes a kettle. Yah. A kettle.
Interviewer: Who worded in the kitchens?
Interviewee: I don’t know. Who was near the kitchen? We have been put in a certain place.. a very long corridor. We didn’t go...even know where the kitchen.. later on, already, it was kitchens.. I think He scrubbed once somewheres.. we didn’t have.. he was in the worst camp.. we were in the worst camp. In the worst camp. Did you clean a kettle? And get a little? I am sorry, I don’t know, I don’t make sense.
Interviewer: How long were you in Kaiservald?
Interviewee: In Kaiservald? Later on, they segregated us, and I was working there. It was with the canisters.
Interviewer: But you can’t remember how long you were there?
Interviewee: It couldn’t have been too long, because they gave us right away what to do. I am talking about Kaiservald. Not right away, I ran away.
Interviewer: So you were there several years, if I understand correctly.
Interviewee: No, about a year and a half. And, then I went to the church. I ran away.
Interviewer: How did you get out?
Interviewee: Do you now. There was a man who used to come to pick us up for working, and, I don’t know, why me...there were so many beautiful girls.. he used to bring something.. nobody should know.. he put.. I never got it, because all the girls.. Jewish girls.
Interviewer: What did he bring?
Interviewee: A piece of bread or something.
Interviewer: A little extra fruit?
Interviewee: We didn’t have any fruit. A piece of bread or something. I never had, and when he saw that I have nothing — I don’t know why — he wanted to help me — Edmund — he told me later on — that’s a long story — it is a book. And, he is also Jewish. But he had a best friend, a Christian, dying and he gave him his papers. He was a writer, a very fine gentleman, and he had.. what did I want to say.
Interviewer: The hauptmann was the head there?
Interviewee: Edmund, right. Edmund. Isn’t it in the book? Anyway, he was Working for the hauptmann, and once he said that he has to clean the apartment and who is coming — a putzfrau- a woman who cleans — he told this to the hauptmann. So, the hauptmann came where I was working, and called my name and I came and now I said, “This is the hundred years of my life, finished.. “ and he said, “You come with me. Tomorrow you are coming to me to clean the apartment.” I said, “Yah vohl, Ya vohl.” I didn’t know him. He was a very affable man, because he was once also victim and he was in camp by the Russians by the Russians arrested. I came. I said, “herr, where is the work for me?” everything was clean. He was cleaning the whole night.. Edmund.. he gave me a pair of trousers to sew up buttons and I came there several times. Several times the same button was cut and I felt very uncomfortable. He put on the table what you could only desire, and I couldn’t eat.. couldn’t. then he goes to the huptman and he said, that I don’t eat anything. Anyway, I couldn’t. and, “Thank you very much” then I used to bring something to one sick woman. A young lady.
Interviewer: You brought food from his house to someone?
Interviewee: Yah, something. I couldn’t. because you have to go to the door. And, I got 25 on my back.
Interviewer: 25 lashes?
Interviewee: 25 lashes because they found it here under my kerchief. Something for her. She had cancer. And said, “You will bring me this and this.” And she used to say, “I’ll be all right.” Anyway, I tried,
Interviewer: Your husband is sitting here so quietly.
Interviewee: He can’t stand how I talk.
Interviewer: You are doing the best you can, and that’s fine.
Interviewee: What do you have questions for me?
Interviewer: Well, I want to know what happened after...how did you get out of Kaiservald? You said you escaped form there. How did you escape?
Interviewee: I ran away. He helped me. He helped me. Edmund helped me.
Interviewer: In what way did he help you?
Interviewee: He a child, a baby daughter. Edmund by the Judge, this and the.. I have a little baby left by the.. and he.. and he said, “How about he should come and pick you up from here?” so, I don’t know how it happened, I don’t remember.
Interviewer: So it wasn’t like you had to escape over the barbed wire fence.
Interviewee: No, no. it was not like.. no fences, no.
Interviewer: In a wagon, or, how did you get out?
Interviewee: This man, who had my baby, he was, he came. He said, “What could be better to do, as to have a mother, a real mother, with the baby.” He came to Riga.. with the baby.
Interviewer: How long had you been separated from your baby?
Interviewee: Oh, a long time,
Interviewer: That’s a long time.
Interviewee: he didn’t have such a aristocratic face. He had a very good heart, and he was.. his mother — the judge’s mother was a housekeeper by a Jewish doctor.
Interviewer: This was a Gentile judge, of course.
Interviewee: Of course.
Interviewer: How did he happen to be the one who took your child?
Interviewee: That’s another thing. I met the doctor once, you know. His daughter got killed, and he introduced me. Everybody was very good tome. Everybody and he picked up.
Interviewer: Did you have any contact or knowledge of your sister and brothers and parents during this time?
Interviewee: I had knowledge that they are not alive.
Interviewer: You knew what they had been killed?
Interviewee: It cannot be nothing else. Pinale, that was a place. Near us. Pinale. Near Vilna. Right near Vilna, because nobody will know it. and now in Israel is a Ukranian man. A different story.
Interviewer: You mean, Mr. Dejmaniak?
Interviewee: Dejmaniak.
Interviewer: He comes from the same city I came from.
Interviewee: Yeah, from where?
Interviewer: Cleveland.
Interviewee: He should never had been born. You know what he did? I don’t want to tell. He used to put screw drivers...
Interviewer: Now we are taping again. Tell me, how was it possible to keep yourself clean in the camp?
Interviewee: It was very bad. But, I was.. I had a good fundament.. you understand?
Interviewer: Fundamental?
Interviewee: Fundamental, yeah, I was good, and young, of course. A lot of people had been eating mushrooms from, excuse me, what a dog did something.. a mushroom grows and they all had abscesses. I did not have one abscess, not one, nothing. It was like this. There was a barn, and full of snow around, crosswind, and it was cold and full of snow.. but, what they dripped the water, not gave a shower, but water was dripping.
Interviewer: You took advantage of that to keep as clean as you could.
Interviewee: Of course. I did as good as I could... I could. But if you would see the bodies of the women. Oh, god, oh god, full of abscesses.. full.. young women. Terrible. Terrible. Interviewer: That was important to surviving.
Interviewee: Was not enough water because it was dripping, dripping.
Interviewer: I have had other people tell me the same thing. So, after you left Kaiservald, then you lived in this church?
Interviewee: No, I didn’t get to Kaiservald yet. I went to this church and hide myself in the church. Two French women, speaking among themselves, and I told them the story in French, but I had a governess when I was young, and I knew the language better than English. And, asked them whether they knew my husband, and I said, I have to come here, and I said, maybe they could give me shelter for the night. From the beginning they wanted to, they after, they said, “we don’t know who you are. We don’t know who you are”
Interviewer: They refused to help you.
Interviewee: Yah. Yes, I came to wait for the judge, no?
Interviewer: How far was this away from Kaiservald?
Interviewee: oh, it was far. It was far. It was Lithuania, and this was Latvia.
Interviewer: How did you get there — from Lithuania to Latvia?
Interviewee: What do you mean?
Interviewer: Did you go in a car?
Interviewee: I told you they had brought us in a cattle car And some German said, “I think I know this one”. My heart was under my eyes already.
Interviewer: I can imagine. You must have been terrified.
Interviewee: I am sorry, how I talk today. I am..
Interviewer: What was it like to be reunited with your child?
Interviewee: It was a long time later. A very long time later. And he told her that there would come a woman.. a beggar. Me. As a beggar. You don’t open the door. She was already here. He kept her very nice. Very nice. But later on she got pregnant. They had been very nice people. Very nice people.
Interviewer: So, then, did you.. I’m not sure how much time passed from the time you were at the camp until the time you got back with your daughter.
Interviewee: Wait.. they arrested me and I was in Gestapo. ok. why don’t you say that I came... let me tell you, this Mr. Edmund, what I told you brought me, and he said the first man in my story, he stole from the hauptmann for whom he was working, a pair of glasses, I should mask myself. He put a puchle, something like this, I should be a hunchback and he did whatever he could for me, and I think that he was not alive today. Edmund? oh, then we are going back? anyway, he came to the hotel, and he met Mr. Edmund, and he pretended that he come to buy whiskey. He had some whiskey. I don’t know what. He was always.. and they call him.. he was afraid — he was a Jew, you know. He was afraid to be connected with anybody since they said that he is crazy. He was always in the library. He was a very intelligent person. He complete so muchbooks. And, he said always, “abens” he is “farticht” rich, he is crazy.. anyways, so what did I want to say? they judge came from Vilna to Riga.
Interviewer: And then he took you with him?
Interviewee: No. not right away. it was said that if somebody will escape then then, this who knew us...this will be killed. And, I said, I will never do this to Edmund. And, I did not go. You see, he went back the first time. He came twice.
Interviewer: He went back to the camp?
Interviewee: and I said that I am not going. He said to me, “What do you think? Maybe his hands are full of blood of your parents and sister and brother, and you, what is the matter with you? I was afraid, and I never prayed for good or bad.
Interviewer: That’s a nice expression. I like that.
Interviewee:. I’ll tell you how it was. They put on all the Jewish girls, your beautiful girls...
Interviewer: This was in the camp?
Interviewee: In the camp. You see, with long hair, all kinds of hair, and undressed. And everybody who was, I don’t know what, a super, he put on a white coat and pretend to be doctors. One bulled the breasts from another. The one scooped the hair from.. Oh, my God, my God, what we went through.
Interviewer: Very humiliating.
Interviewee: Anyway, we had been worse than cattle. It was a sign in Vilna for killing a Jew and a dog — no punishment.
Interviewer: There was no punishment for killing a Jew or a dog.
Interviewee: Or a dog or a Jew, the same — no punishment. It would be a good thing. What else? Today I have Help me. ah, Edmund, I would give him what I have. He was better than a thousand brothers.
Interviewer: That must have been a terrifying time for you.
Interviewee: it was only being so strong as I was and so young as I am that I could survive, believe me. Yeah, you know who.. used to deliver to my parents, chickens and eggs and everything,
Interviewer: With all the disguise, they recognized you?
Interviewee: I took off.. who could breath? But they recognized me. I said, what are you talking about? Interviewer: So the women got off of the train, but they didn’t report you?
Interviewee: I said, “What are you talking about? It’s ridiculous. I belong to this little town.. to the village. Anyway, they went out first and they didn’t report. I don’t think that they would know. Anyway, so, what did I want to say? Then, this Mr. Hall was a millionaire, and he was also cholem.. Vilna and everybody who knows... Vilna knows who is going. He was also hiding by the same judge. And two other girls. One, the daughter of a big, big book store, and one Lithuanian. And all of us.. and he used to say, Floor, if we survive, money is water, like water is full, and he has “mir zagen” and he had a lot. We’ll make all, in all the cities, but give me your hand, and you will walk with me.”
Interviewer: To do what?
Interviewee: To let know, to let the whole world know what they did to us.
Interviewer: What happened.
Interviewee: I said, I’ll give you my hand. In Jewish, “kiashaf”, is more than ever — like you swear, and I gave him my hand that I will help him. I didn’t have anybody in the whole world and I wanted all the world should know.
Interviewer: So the judge never had.. the man that you are talking about.. you little girl.. and two other people and yourself.. five people —hidden under his roof. Didn’t people wonder about this?
Interviewee: Who would know.. nobody walked out.
Interviewer: But he had to bring in food for everybody.
Interviewee: They had food.. the Lithuanian people had food — full of special places where they had. This was nothing. But, this lady, the wife of Mr. Rutkowska, his name is Rutkowska... this judge. The lady, Lisa. Anyway, Lisa used to take out the baby a little for the fresh air. They put wonderful flowers in her room and everything — but still a little fresh air. And everybody said, “Whose child is this? Beautiful child. Such eyes.” Not veiled. You have to know that the Lithuanian people are very ugly. Ugly.
Interviewer: So, a beautiful child was unusual.
Interviewee: That it’s probably Jewish. So, it was on a day of my birthday, a knock on the door. I sleep with my child in the bed. The two girls sleeping there. A terrible, terrible knocking at the door. He liked to take a little drink. He liked to drink, the judge. He gave me a name, Gemma. Not Floor, Gemma. He screams, “Somebody at the door, Gemma, Gemma, Gemma. I don’t trust him. I stay still. And she took out the baby and she was walking. Opened the door. They came.
Interviewer: Who came?
Interviewee: Two Gestaop. With a bid dog. The girls right away spoke beautiful Lithuanian, because they are from there. I don’t know one word. Before they came in, she said, Floor, call something, do something. You don’t know one word. We speak so fluently” didn’t help them. Anyway, they came in with the dog, and my shoe was, by this time four and a half, small, and the dog took my shoe and the one Gestapo said, “Whose little shoe is this?” and she.. the Lithuanians have such big feet...
Interviewer: Peasant feet.
Interviewee: They are peasants. Anyway, she said, “This is mine” But he didn’t pay attention. And the girls, they spoke to him Lithuanian and it didn’t help. He told them to get out. And she took the baby. And, I am alone in the bed. And she took all the heavy mattresses, the heavy.. and springs.. you know.. and put them on me.
Interviewer: Put them on top of you?
Interviewee: On top of me. I was in the bed. And on top of me they should see me. I would be here. Anyway, to make a long story short, finally, with troubles and troubles, she started screaming to them, “This is my child, and how dare you.. “ And she spoke to the child all kinds of words, but she didn’t realize. She didn’t answer nothing.
Interviewer: How old was she?
Interviewee: A year maybe, already. About a year. So, they went, and they said they are coming back. If I would listen to him, if I wouldn’t use my own judgment. I should jump to him, I wouldn’t be here. Because I don’t. anyway, to make a long story short, they went away, and right away he went down and bought a paper. And, in the paper was announcement, to the Germans, they need a putz frau who cleans, and this and this and this. And, I went, and I told them.. Riga, that’s right.
Interviewer: So you took a job as a housekeeper.
Interviewee: Not keeper. To clean the floors, to clean the dust out. A putzfrau, cleaning. Anyway, then, what did I want to say.. then I came and I went right away to this.. Each German had a Geliebte. A Geliebte means a girl-friend. And, I probably didn’t look like a.. anyway, I had troubles. I had to clean, to wash and this.. and this was everything not enough.. not enough.
Interviewer: And where did you live then?
Interviewee: They game me some place.
Interviewer: In the same house where you did the work?
Interviewee: Yes, there was plenty of little rooms and everything Later on I knew that one Russian woman, and I speak very well Russian — I know Russian, anyway. That she would gladly take me to help me. I said, “I’ll give you money when I’ll get it, but I haven’t got it now.” Come on, And I was.. when I used to finish the job, I was happy to be in a different atmosphere. You know, for a long time, knowing very well German, I couldn’t hear one word German. I, right away, saw pictures of this bitter man with the black, with the black. Huh?. There is everything in my head. Yah.
Interviewer: That’s all right. You are sharing your memories with us as well as your experiences.
Interviewee: That’s terrible. Anyway, I was living there.
Interviewer: How long did you stay there?
Interviewee: then, one Oberfurdoktor, that is, a higher doctor who was working for them — they have a lot of Russian soldiers with a half of face. This, I had the right to give to them an injection or to make, or to do something for them — but not to the Germans I used to come out..
Interviewer: The Russians were prisoners?
Interviewee: Of course, prisoners. Treated horrible. Anyway, then, he said that I should.. um.. work by blutlisen Interviewer: Laboratory work?
Interviewee: To could the blood cells and everything. I said, but I don’t know how. I said, I am only a putzfru. But you will learn he said. By us, a putzfrau knows everything. Knows languages. What should I tell you? You see, I learned. I knew before a little.
Interviewer: it must have been a little easier to do that then to be cleaning.
Interviewee: Yes. It was later, but I almost paid with my life for that. And, I was working there and I got.. I was very undernourished and some of the Germans gave me cod liver oil to drink and something soups and something to eat, and whatever he could — he.. one or another who cooked, used to bring.. and I started blooming. You know. With the food. So the Oberschutz, doctor said he wants to go out with me. And this started my troubles. I finished very bad and was arrested to the Gestapo, you know. I was.. I feel.. I had terrible feelings and I said to the lady in Russian that I have a very bad feeling that something is happening to me. And, all of a sudden, came a jeep, with how many, I don’t now, how many it was there soldiers.
Interviewer: I’m sorry. All of a sudden came what?
Interviewee: A jeep. You know what is a jeep? NO. Interviewer: A jeep, OK
Interviewee: A jeep with men. I’m sorry. With men. A couple of men with such big carabines — what is that? machine guns.. and took me away. I was afraid that this is the end of my life. Anyway, but what can I do? But, I didn’t.. but they gave me a little cell. In the morning, I’ll go to the district attorney. So,
Interviewer: Did they tell you why they took you away?
Interviewee: No. they took me away.. that’s the end.
Interviewer: They didn’t have to tell you?
Interviewee: No, they didn’t have to tell me. All night I was knocking on the door, knocking in the door from the cell, but nobody came there. Five o’clock came. “wait another hour and you’ll go to the District Attorney.” So, came the hour and they brought me to the District Attorney. I decided not to answer him what he is asking me. I said, “Ich nicht Deutsch” that’s not an expression in German, “Ich nicht Deutch” I said, “Ich nicht Deutch” I have to describe you the room. The room was very big, very long. In each corner sat one District Attorney. One dog. In all corners, four. On one wall was a big board, you know, on what you could write, and it was a big.. how you call it a big whip, full still with blood, from the people who had been beaten. And I said to him.. he asked me, “you are a student? And this, and that, and this.. “ and anyway, I said, “Ich nicht Deutch” everything was noticed by one man who sat, I was here, he was up there, and he came over. “Was is loes?” What happened? He said, “Which language do you speak? I said, “Polish” and he was a Pole. I said, “Polish. I attended Polish University and I speak Polish.” So, he came and he said, and I talked to him — mind district attorney doesn’t understand a word. But I said, “this is a private affair” not dispute: no. Privately I paid for this, because I didn’t want to go out with him.
